voyage.title: Drake's Circumnavigation (1577-1580)
voyage.sponsor: sailing from Plymouth under a commission from Elizabeth I kept deliberately vague
voyage.summary: The second circumnavigation and the first by a captain who survived it: south to Port San Julián and the execution of Thomas Doughty, through the Strait, up the Pacific coast raiding Spanish shipping, a landing on the California coast he called Nova Albion, then west across the Pacific and home by the Cape.
voyage.what_was_lost: Drake published nothing. This account was compiled in 1628 by his nephew from the notes of Francis Fletcher, the chaplain — whose original manuscript is lost, and who quarrelled with Drake on the voyage. The queen ordered the expedition's charts and journals surrendered and kept secret, so what survives is a family's version of a state secret, fifty years late.

waypoints.event: Sir Francis Drake set sail from Plymouth with a fleet of five ships and 164 men, beginning his famous circumnavigation voyage. However, contrary winds forced the fleet to put into Falmouth the next day.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: The 15 day of Nouembre, in the yeere of our Lord 1577, M, Francis Drahe, with, a fleete of fiue ships and barkes, and to the number of 164 men, gentlemen, and sailers, departed from Plimmouth, gluing out his pretended uoyage for Alexandria : but the wind falling contrary, hee was forced the next morning to put into Falmouth hauen, in Cornewall, where such and so terrible a tempest tooke vs, as few men haue scene the like, and was indeed so vehement, that all our ships were like to haue gone to wracke : but it pleased God to preserue us from that extremitie, and to afflict us onely for that present with these two particulars.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (Hakluyt Society, 1854)

waypoints.event: The expedition sighted the coast of Brazil near latitude 31°30' south, observing fires made by the inhabitants and noting the low land near the sea. This marked their first landfall in South America after a long crossing from Cape Verde.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: Passing thus, in beholding the most excellent works of the eternall God in the seas, as if we had beene in a garden of pleasure, April 5, we fell with the coast of Brasill, in 31 deg. 30 min., towards the pole Antartick, where the land is lowe neere the sea, but much higher within the countrie, hauing in depth not aboue 12 fathome, 3 leagues off from the shoare, and being descried by the inhabitants, we sawe great and huge fires made by them in sundry places, which order of making fires, though it be vniversall, as well among Christians as heathens, yet it is not likely that many doe vse it to that end which the Brasilians doe : to wit, for a sacri- fice to deuills, whereat they intermixe many and diuers ceremonies of coniurati

waypoints.event: Drake's expedition arrived at the Rio de la Plata, where they went ashore and obtained fresh water before continuing their voyage.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: where they went on land, and prouided themselues of fresh water.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (Hakluyt Society, 1854)

waypoints.place_modern: Puerto San Julián, Santa Cruz, Argentina
waypoints.event: Drake's fleet arrived at Port S. Julian, where a trial was held for Mr. Thomas Doughty, who was convicted of mutiny and executed in the presence of the crew.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: The port of it to be the same which Magellan named Port S. Julian : for we Sant Julian. " found a gybbet on an hil, whereupon they were executed that did conspire against Magellan, and certaine bones also of their dead bodies. The 22 of this moneth our Generall going to shore upon the maine with 7 or 8 of his men, met with 3 of the Paia- gons hauing bowes and arrowes, who came neere to our me min sia^ne making them signes to depart.

waypoints.event: Drake's expedition entered the Strait of Magellan, observing the tides and currents and noting the geography of the passage as they navigated from the Atlantic towards the Pacific.

waypoints.event: Drake and his crew, guided by an Indian pilot, arrived and anchored at the harbor of Valparaiso, which the Spaniards called Valperizo, on December 5th, 1578.
waypoints.diary_excerpt:
and so the 5 day after our arriuall, viz., December 4, we departed hence, and the next day, December 5, by the willing conduct of our new Indian Pilote, we came to anchor in the desired harbor.

waypoints.event: Drake arrived at the port of Arica, where he found a ship carrying thirteen thousand pezos of silver, took the silver, burned the ship, and decided not to land after seeing Spanish horsemen and footmen on shore.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: At this port of Arica he found a ship that had in her thirteene thousand pezos of siluer, which hauing taken out, he burned the sayd ship, and after thought to haue landed ; but seeing both horsemen and footemen on shore hee would not, but proceeded on his voy- age.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (Hakluyt Society, 1854)

waypoints.event: Drake's crew captured the treasure-laden Spanish ship Cacafuego off Cape de San Francisco, seizing large quantities of gold, silver, and jewels.
waypoints.diary_excerpt:
The place where we tooke this prize, was ' called Cape de San Francisco, about one hundred and fiftie , leagues from Panama.
The pilots name of this shippe was Francisco, and amongst other plate that our Generall found in this ship, he found two very faire guilt bowles of siluer, which were the pilots : to whom our Generall sayd : Senior Pilot, you haue here two siluer cups, but I must needes haue one of them ; which the pilot, because hee could not otherwise chuse, yeelded unto, and gaue the other to the steward of our generals ships.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (Hakluyt Society, 1854)

waypoints.place_modern: Pearl Islands, Gulf of Panama, Panama

waypoints.event: Sir Francis Drake landed at a fair and goodly haven on the northwest coast of California, where he stayed several weeks, took possession of the land in the name of Queen Elizabeth, and named it Nova Albion.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: where, finding a fair e and goodly hauen, he landed, and staying there inany weekes, and discouering many excellent things in the countrey, and great shelve of rich minerall matter, and heing offered the dominion of the countrey hy the Lord of the same, hee tooke possession thereof in the behalf e of her Maies- tie, and named it Noua Albion.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (Hakluyt Society, 1854)

waypoints.event: Drake's ship crossed the mid-Pacific Ocean, sailing for 68 days without sight of land before reaching islands north of the equator.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: And so hauing nothing in our view but aire and sea, without sight of any land for the space of full 68 dayes together, wee continued our course through the maine Ocean, till Septcm- her oO following, on which day we fell in kenne of certaine Hands, lying about eight degrees to the Northward of the line.

waypoints.event: Drake's expedition arrived at the Moluccas and was met by the Vice-King of Ternate, who invited them to visit the King of Ternate and assured them of a warm welcome.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: The 14. of November we fell with the Islands of Maluco, which day at night (hauing directed our course to runne with Tydore) in coasting along the Island of Mutyr, belonging to the King of Ternate, his Deputie or Vice-King seeing us at sea, came with his canoa to us without all feare, and came aboard ; and after some conference with our Generall, willed him in any wise to runne in with Ternate, and not with Tydore, assuring him that the King would bee glad of his comming, and would be ready to doe what he would require; for which purpose he himselfe would that night be with the King, and tell him the newes, with whom, if he once dealt, hee should finde that as he was a King, so his word should stand : adding further, that if he

waypoints.event: Drake and his crew arrived at the island of Java, where they traded with the local people for rice, daggers, plantains, coconuts, sugar canes, and fresh water before continuing their voyage toward the Cape of Good Hope.
